context: ROAD-R adds explicit logical requirements to ROAD and studies learning and prediction mechanisms that use those requirements \cite{road-r}. This distinguishes two meanings of structure. Logical requirements specify which combinations are admissible; semantic representations describe similarities between class meanings. Encouraging constraint satisfaction during training is also different from enforcing admissibility at prediction time. A classifier may produce logically compatible outputs while failing to recognize the correct event. Conversely, improved average precision does not guarantee consistency between primitive and composition predictions. The semantic classifier therefore addresses recognition and does not claim the guarantees of a constrained-output method.

context: Several approaches adjust how class frequency enters the learning objective. Cui et al. derive class-balanced weights from the effective number of samples, reflecting diminishing additional information as the number of examples grows \cite{class-balanced}. Cao et al. introduce a label-distribution-aware margin and defer reweighting until after an initial representation-learning period \cite{ldam}. Both methods use class frequency, but they intervene differently: one changes the contribution of examples, while the other changes class-dependent margins and the training schedule. For this study, these distinctions reinforce the need to define tail membership from training data and to keep that definition fixed during evaluation.

They therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to a classifier whose phrase matrix remains frozen. For this thesis, their main implication is that the choice and adaptation of class descriptions must be documented and controlled.

context: Adaptation can also use labeled visual examples directly. Tip-Adapter builds a key--value cache from a few-shot training set and combines feature retrieval with the pretrained model's predictions \cite{tip-adapter}. context: Transferring image--text models to video introduces temporal design choices. X-CLIP uses cross-frame attention and video-dependent prompting to adapt pretrained image--language representations to video recognition \cite{xclip}. Together, these studies caution against attributing an improvement to semantic reasoning merely because a vision--language model is involved. Temporal processing, adaptation, and pooling can each contribute.

context: Compositional recognition asks how predictions for parts relate to predictions for their combinations. ROAD considers both direct composite prediction and composition of primitive scores \cite{road}. The developed MLP follows the former goal through a structured input: it receives primitive predictions together with visual features and learns scores for the benchmark's valid duplexes and triplets. This gives it access to relationships that a fixed product or minimum of primitive scores cannot adapt to the task. It does not impose logical agreement between independently predicted heads.

context: Figure~\ref{fig:frame-map} shows how a scored box contributes to this metric. For each class, the evaluator processes detections in descending score order within a frame and matches each detection to an available ground-truth box of that class when IoU is at least 0.5. Each ground-truth box can be matched once. Unmatched detections, including duplicate detections after a ground-truth box has been consumed, count as false positives. The evaluator then ranks detections across the selected frames to obtain a precision--recall curve. It integrates the interpolated precision envelope at changes in recall and averages AP over the classes in the reported group. This follows the detection-evaluation principles of PASCAL VOC \cite{voc}; the actual implementation is the ROAD baseline evaluator \cite{road}.

context: The final CSEB uses the released InternVideo2-CLIP-1B system \cite{internvideo2-clip-1b}.
